traits: Fifteen pairs of very long legs — moves in a fast, ghostly blur
Found in tubs and sinks it can’t climb out of
Yellowish-gray with dark stripes running down the body
Always running away from you, not toward you

look_alikes.difference: House centipedes have extremely long, thread-like legs and blur when moving; Florida blue centipedes have short legs and move deliberately.

copy.fact: It actively hunts roaches, silverfish, and moths at night — an unpaid exterminator with too many legs.
copy.blurb: If you can stand it, it’s working for you. If you can’t, cup-and-release counts.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator; indicates other insect prey present. No treatment needed unless customer wants it excluded; check bathroom/garage moisture entry points.

traits: Coils into a tight spiral when touched
Slow, round-bodied, legs ripple in waves as it moves
Two pairs of legs per body segment (versus one pair for centipedes)
Shows up in large numbers after soaking rain

look_alikes.difference: Millipedes have two short leg pairs per segment and coil when touched; house centipedes have one very long leg pair per segment and move fast.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from the side, counting legs per body segment.

copy.what_it_means: A composting machine that recycles dead leaves into soil. Heavy rain floods the leaf litter and pushes them onto the lanai. It can release a mild defensive secretion, so sweep it out rather than pick it up; indoors it usually dries out, and repeat visitors point to a damp spot near the door.
copy.fact: A composting machine — it recycles dead leaves into soil. Rain floods the leaf litter and evicts them onto your lanai.
copy.blurb: They rarely survive long indoors. Sweep them out rather than handling them, and if they keep coming in, look for damp spots near doors.

tech_notes: Rain-driven seasonal migration from mulch/leaf litter. Defensive secretion can mildly irritate skin/eyes on contact; advise sweeping rather than handling. Exterior perimeter treatment + reducing mulch-to-foundation contact handles recurring waves.

traits: Rolls into a perfect ball when disturbed
Gray, armored, oval, about half an inch, under pots and stepping stones
Needs consistent dampness — dies quickly indoors
A land crustacean, not an insect — breathes through gill-like organs

look_alikes.difference: Pillbugs roll into a tight ball and have no tail appendages; sowbugs cannot roll up and have two small tail-like appendages at the rear.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the rear end for tail appendages, and whether it can roll into a ball.

copy.what_it_means: A land crustacean, not an insect — it breathes through gill-like organs, a tiny armored cousin of a shrimp. Mainly beneficial in the garden; it occasionally wanders indoors but causes no structural damage.
copy.fact: Not an insect at all — it’s a land crustacean that breathes through gill-like organs, a tiny armored shrimp cousin.
copy.blurb: A drainage indicator more than a pest. Kids’ favorite yard animal.

tech_notes: Beneficial decomposer; occasional indoor wanderer tied to moisture. No treatment usually needed; exterior perimeter if numerous indoors.

traits: Elongated, flattened body about 1.5 to 2 inches long, often described with a bluish-black sheen and orange-yellow head and legs
One pair of legs per body segment, with the last pair noticeably longer and trailing behind
Moves in fast, darting bursts rather than a steady crawl
Found under bark, logs, mulch or stones by day, hunting insects and spiders at night

look_alikes.difference: Centipede has one pair of legs per segment, moves fast, and can bite; millipede has two pairs per segment, moves slowly, and doesn't bite

safety_line: Its bite can hurt like a bee sting for a short while but isn't dangerous to a healthy adult; see a doctor if you have a bigger reaction or are prone to allergies.

copy.what_it_means: A predator that actually helps by eating other insects and spiders around the yard. It only bites if picked up or cornered, so the main reason to treat is simply not wanting to run into one barehanded near the house.
copy.fact: Despite the bite, it's doing pest control of its own outdoors, hunting roaches, crickets and other small insects at night.

tech_notes: Confirm leg-pair-per-segment count and coloring to distinguish from millipedes; reducing harborage (leaf litter, log piles, dense mulch against the foundation) reduces indoor encounters more than a pesticide alone.

review.notes: UF/IFAS EDIS IG093 (Household/occasional invaders) was checked directly and covers centipedes only as a group ("usually brownish, flattened animals"), with no mention of this species or blue coloring; UF/IFAS's Featured Creatures collection (771 titles checked) has no dedicated page for Hemiscolopendra marginata. "Florida Blue Centipede" is the fixed common name from the project's master slug list, not this worker's choice; the bluish-black coloring itself is from general reference material, not a UF/IFAS/FWC/FDACS source. Re-checked this session: a peer-reviewed taxonomic revision exists (Shelley, in Hoffman & Shelley 1996 / a later genus revision redescribing H. marginata), and a USFWS species page exists for this species, but neither was accessible with a color description in the sources checked; USFWS's page gives only taxonomic/organizational data with no physical description at all. Resolution: the bluish-black coloring is hedged with 'often described' in traits rather than stated as a settled fact, since it is consistently reported across independent photographic references (Wikipedia, and the species' own common/site name) but not confirmed by a UF/IFAS/FWC/FDACS source; this is a purely descriptive, non-safety morphological detail. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

Found under mulch, stones, rotting logs or leaf litter, sometimes wandering into garages in numbers after rain

copy.what_it_means: A harmless decomposer that feeds on decaying leaves and mulch, not living plants. Large numbers after rain, sometimes migrating into garages, mean a moisture/mulch situation, not a pest to worry about. Sweep them up rather than handling them, since the secretion can mildly irritate skin.
copy.fact: When threatened, it curls into a tight coil and releases a defensive secretion that may mildly irritate skin — its only defense, since it has no bite or sting.

tech_notes: Reduce moisture and thin mulch/leaf litter against the foundation as the primary fix; large migrations are usually seasonal and self-limiting.

traits: Oval, flattened, gray body with overlapping armor-like plates, like a tiny land-dwelling isopod
Two short tail-like appendages (uropods) visible at the rear end
Cannot roll into a ball; just scurries away when disturbed
Found in damp mulch, under pots, logs or stones, feeding on decaying plant matter

copy.what_it_means: A harmless decomposer that feeds on decaying mulch and plant matter, not living plants or the house itself. Numbers near the foundation usually mean mulch is piled too deep or too damp, and thinning it out is the real fix.
copy.fact: It breathes through gill-like structures and needs damp surroundings to survive, which is why it's almost never found somewhere dry.

tech_notes: No treatment usually needed; recommend keeping mulch 2 to 4 inches deep and away from direct foundation contact to dry out harborage.
